qualifier: For experienced lawyers, years into practice, who find tech law interesting but suspect the moment to switch has already passed.
symptom_title: It feels like a field for the young
symptom: You have practised for years. You know your courts, your clients and your craft. When tech law comes up, the faces in the photos are young, and the words sound like they belong to another generation. Nobody seems to be speaking to someone at your stage.
Part of you is curious. Part of you says a lawyer at your stage should not be starting from zero, sitting beside fresh graduates and learning new vocabulary.
So you watched, perhaps visited the page, and let it pass. You told yourself it was a career for people with more years ahead of them. Yet the thought keeps returning, which is why you are here.
outcome_title: What changes when experience becomes the advantage
outcome: Tech law is the legal work that technology companies need across their contracts, compliance, privacy, policy and disputes. Much of that work is judgement about risk, and judgement is what years of practice build.

You could add a tech law career to what you already have, advising startups and foreign clients alongside your practice. It is not starting again. It is taking a seasoned skill into a newer market, where clients need someone who has seen how things go wrong.
alternatives_title: What experienced lawyers usually do instead

alternatives.t: Sending tech questions to younger colleagues
alternatives.why: It keeps the client happy for now, but the expertise, and the relationship, slowly move to whoever answers. You remain the lawyer for everything except the growing part.
A long academic course feels thorough, yet it takes years and teaches theory first. At your stage you need practical skills you can put to work while you are still learning.

alternatives.t: Deciding to stay with what you know
alternatives.why: A settled practice is valuable. But staying put by default, rather than by choice, leaves the curiosity unanswered and the option unexplored. Years later, the same question can return with less time to act on it.

reframe_title: The rules are new for everyone
reframe: Most of India's tech rules are recent, so nobody has decades of experience in them. The camp script puts it this way: a veteran and a fresh graduate stand on the same starting line. Only one of them brings years of judgement.

So the question is positioning, not age. You already know how deals go wrong, how clients think and how disputes unfold. Tech companies need exactly that judgement wrapped around their contracts and structures.
cost_title: What it costs to decide it is too late
cost: Deciding it is too late is the one decision that makes it true. The practice continues either way. Three evenings let you test the field from your own chair, with nothing to give up.
role_h2: What tech law work looks like for an experienced lawyer
role: Structuring is a natural fit. A startup asks whether its business can be done at all, in which jurisdiction and at what cost. The script's example is a lending-algorithm company that wants to work with banks and NBFCs.

Advisory work suits you too. Founders need someone who has seen deals fail to tell them where their contract, policy or plan is weak. Your years in practice make that advice worth hearing. A young founder rarely has anyone like you on call.

When things go wrong, tech disputes follow: contract arbitrations, consumer and regulatory complaints, impersonation and takedown fights. You bring a litigator's or adviser's instinct to a field that is still young. The disputes are new, but the instinct for how a case turns is not.
first_artifact: On Day 3 you see how a blockchain founder's venture is structured as a Wyoming DAO LLC, a company form built for that kind of business. It is a structuring question from start to finish: what form, where, and why. For a lawyer who has advised clients for years, this is familiar thinking applied to a new kind of business. It shows how your existing judgement transfers.
longer_term: The six-month plan from Day 2 asks for about two hours a day, one learning and one on outreach. For an experienced lawyer, outreach can lean on the network you already have. Over six months you could add tech skills steadily and introduce them to clients who already trust you. Some of those clients may already run, or invest in, technology businesses.

faq.q: Will I be the oldest person in the room?
faq.a: The camp is live online, and its priority list includes practising lawyers exploring tech law. You join from your own desk, and the learning is the same for everyone.

faq.q: Is my experience actually useful here?
faq.a: Yes. The script's case is that the rules are new, so nobody has a long head start. What you bring, judgement on risk and on clients, is the part newcomers take years to build. The camp only adds the vocabulary and the documents.

faq.q: Do I need to learn the technology itself?
faq.a: No. The script says the legal work depends on the business model, not on coding. You learn how tech businesses make money and what each model needs.

faq.q: How much time and money does it take to try?
faq.a: Three live evenings, 24 to 26 Oct, for Rs 10 including GST. It is refundable, and there are no recordings.

closing_title: Experienced lawyers: it is not too late for tech law
closing: Experienced lawyers can start tech law at any stage of practice, because the rules are new for everyone. Three live evenings show you the structuring, contracts and advisory work where your judgement counts most. Your years become the head start.
